entries.431b6b73b273c9d1cbfd2c27209ba3a9e58f94f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6378"/><div sID="gen9772" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6378"/><hi type="bold">17-20. yet more--</hi>literally, "added to sin," instead of being led to repentance (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.4">Ro 2:4</reference>). <div eID="gen9772" type="x-p"/>

entries.a440acb615c05599977cb40cce26e2da2fdf216a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6388"/><div sID="gen9786" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6388"/>33-39. entries.542768d493ba3c16ac719cd69226ce4e3d64bea4: <div eID="gen21114" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21115" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21116" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21116" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21115" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21117" type="x-p"/> An enumeration of the principal effects of the goodness of God to his people, vv. 1-16; of their rebellions and punishment, vv. 17-33; their feigned repentance, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.34-Psa.78.37">Psa 78:34-37</reference>; God's compassion towards them, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.39">Psa 78:39</reference>; their backsliding, and forgetfulness of his mercy, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.40-Psa.78.42">Psa 78:40-42</reference>; the plagues which he brought upon the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.43-Psa.78.51">Psa 78:43-51</reference>; the deliverance of his own people, and their repeated ingratitude and disobedience, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.52-Psa.78.58">Psa 78:52-58</reference>; their punishment, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.59-Psa.78.64">Psa 78:59-64</reference>; God's wrath against their adversaries, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.65">Psa 78:65</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.66">Psa 78:66</reference>; his rejection of the tribes of Israel abut his choice of the tribe of Judah, and of David to be king over his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.67-Psa.78.72">Psa 78:67-72</reference>. <div eID="gen21117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21118" type="x-p"/> The title, Maschil of Asaph; or, according to the margin, A Psalm for Asaph to give instruction; contains nothing particular. The Arabic has, "A sermon from Asaph to the people." The Psalm was probably not written by David, but after the separation of the ten tribes of Israel, and after the days of Rehoboam, and before the Babylonish captivity, for the temple was still standing, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.69">Psa 78:69</reference>. Calmet supposes that it was written in the days of Asa, who had gained, by the aid of the Syrians, a great victory over the Israelites; and brought back to the pure worship of God many out of the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon. See 2 Chronicles 15 and <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1-2Chr.16.14">2Chr 16:1-14</reference>. <div eID="gen21118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21119" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21120" type="x-p"/> Give ear, O my people - This is the exordium of this very pathetic and instructive discourse.
entries.fcf16634fd7100668f1927a63dd43a1175da505f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21121" type="x-p"/> In a parable - Or, I will give you instruction by numerous examples; see <reference osisRef="Psa.49.1-Psa.49.4">Psa 49:1-4</reference> (note), which bears a great similarity to this; and see the notes there. The term parable, in its various acceptations, has already been sufficiently explained; but משל mashal may here mean example, as opposed to תורה torah, law or precept, <reference osisRef="Psa.49.1">Psa 49:1</reference>.
entries.3c70a17944efff06a7f0c1700eb6677b8f09e85e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21122" type="x-p"/> Which we have heard and known - We have heard the law, and known the facts.
entries.e9fd890b8b8765ccffa8461798625aa126348249: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21123" type="x-p"/> We will not hide them - In those ancient times there was very little reading, because books were exceedingly scarce; tradition was therefore the only, or nearly the only, means of preserving the memory of past events. They were handed down from father to son by parables or pithy sayings and by chronological poems. This very Psalm is of this kind, and must have been very useful to the Israelites, as giving instructions concerning their ancient history, and recounting the wonderful deeds of the Almighty in their behalf.
entries.bb20ab21eadf48b0e6fb61f606f3b2b53ebb499d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21124" type="x-p"/> A testimony in Jocob - This may signify the various ordinances, rites, and ceremonies prescribed by the law; and the word law may mean the moral law, or system of religious instruction, teaching them their duty to God, to their neighbor, and to themselves. These were commanded to the fathers - the patriarchs and primitive Hebrews, that they should make them known to their children, who should make them known to the generation that was to come, whose children should also be instructed that they might declare them to their children; to the end that their hope might be in God, that they might not forget his works, and might keep his commandments: that they might not be as their fathers, but have their heart right and their spirit steadfast with God, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.6-Psa.78.8">Psa 78:6-8</reference>. Five generations appear to be mentioned above: 1. Fathers; 2. Their children; 3. The generation to come; 4. And their children; 5. And their children. They were never to lose sight of their history throughout all their generations. Some think the testimony here may mean the tabernacle.
entries.7cda94c632e19b5d83ce5e8f13cffaf80e179d8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21125" type="x-p"/> The children of Ephraim - turned back - This refers to some defeat of the Ephraimites; and some think to that by the men of Gath, mentioned <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.21">1Chr 7:21</reference>. R. D. Kimchi says this defeat of the Ephraimites was in the desert; and although the story be not mentioned in the law, yet it is written in the Books of the Chronicles, where we read, on the occasion of "Zabad the Ephraimite, and Shuthelah, etc., whom the men of Gath, who were born in the land, slew; and Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brethren came to comfort him," <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.20-1Chr.7.22">1Chr 7:20-22</reference> : but to what defeat of the Ephraimites this refers is not certainly known; probably the Israelites after the division of the two kingdoms are intended.
entries.45187e9c1ae8321367975101c633f5fec510f6d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21126" type="x-p"/> They kept not the covenant; of God - They abandoned his worship, both moral and ritual. Thev acted like the Ephraimites in the above case, who threw down their bows and arrows, and ran away.
entries.3ed4fe16d1428a9047381fbe1e0b76406b4cb84b: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21127" type="x-p"/> The field of Zoan - "In campo Taneos," Vugate. Tanis was the capital of Pharaoh, where Moses wrought so many miracles. It was situated in the Delta, on one of the most easterly branches of the Nile. It was afterwards called Thanis; and from it the district was called the Thanitic Canton. See Calmet. Dr. Shaw thinks Zoan was intended to signify Egypt in general.
entries.1f0500679da9b1efc2f056a7ecdc07b5ecf0e224: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21128" type="x-p"/> He divided the sea, and caused them to pass through - The reader is requested to consult the notes on the parallel passages marked in the margin on this verse and <reference osisRef="Psa.78.14-Psa.78.17">Psa 78:14-17</reference>, etc., where all these miracles are largely explained.
entries.026b832aa87ebc42b060bc1dbd56203d87cfb7a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen21128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21129" type="x-p"/> By asking meat for their lust - לנפשם lenaphsham, "for their souls," i.e., for their lives; for they said in their hearts that the light bread, the manna, was not sufficient to sustain their natural force, and preserve their lives. It seems, however, from the expression, that they were wholly carnal; that they had no spirituality of mind; they were earthly, animal, and devilish.
entries.59c713c4ffd819deed7fdd07bbf010b7c1040190: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen21129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21130" type="x-p"/> They believed not in God - After all the miracles they had seen, they were not convinced that there was a Supreme Being! and, consequently, they did not trust in his salvation - did not expect the glorious rest which he had promised them. Their descendants in the present day are precisely in this state. Multitudes of them disbelieve the Divine origin of their law, and have given up all hopes of a Messiah.
entries.dab6f0ce09fdc71a41c543614021174d77b5dad8: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen21130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21131" type="x-p"/> The corn of heaven - The manna. It fell about their camp in the form of seeds; and as it appeared to come down from the clouds, it was not improperly termed heavenly corn, or heavenly grain, דגן שמים degan shamayim. The word shamayim is frequently taken to express the atmosphere.
entries.125e7945db1dc7ed5caaeb8d0129f1def76c9e68: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen21131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21132" type="x-p"/> Man did eat angels' food - לחם אבירים אכל איש lechem abbirim achal ish, "Man did eat the bread of the mighty ones;" or, each person ate, etc. They ate such bread as could only be expected at the tables of the rich and great, the best, the most delicate food. How little did this gross people know of the sublime excellence of that which they called light bread, and which they said their soul loathed; <reference osisRef="Num.21.5">Num 21:5</reference>! It was a type of Jesus Christ for so says St. Paul: "They all ate the same spiritual meat, and drank the same spiritual drink," etc., <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.3">1Cor 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.4">1Cor 10:4</reference>. And our Lord calls himself "the bread that came down from heaven, that giveth life unto the world," <reference osisRef="Joh.6.31-Joh.6.35">Joh 6:31-35</reference> : but a Jew sees nothing but with the eyes of flesh. It is true their doctors or rabbins are full of allegories, mysteries, and conceits; but they are, in general, such as would disgrace the Cabinet des Fees, and would not be tolerated in the nursery. O, how thick a veil hangs over their gross and hardened hearts.
entries.6377db14427c45e6b04fc5cf2ea6d306018ee3ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen21132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21133" type="x-p"/> He caused an east wind to blow - See the note on <reference osisRef="Num.11.31">Num 11:31</reference>.
entries.efd64b53aeecaffd4a5cadb10f15c465e5630268: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen21133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21134" type="x-p"/> For all this they sinned still - How astonishing is this! They were neither drawn by mercies, nor awed by judgments! But we shall cease to wonder at this, if we have a thorough acquaintance with our own hearts.
entries.8631df95a9b3c59d269f0f9464d9c2c6fa856c85: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen21134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21135" type="x-p"/> Their days did he consume in vanity - By causing them to wander forty years in the wilderness, vainly expecting an end to their labor, and the enjoyment of the promised rest, which, by their rebellions, they had forfeited.
entries.fdc0cbbf11de0544078dd58c048b0da6b57051d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen21135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21136" type="x-p"/> When he slew them - While his judgments were upon them, then they began to humble themselves, and deprecate his wrath. When they saw some fall, the rest began to tremble.
entries.5192a1b04d103f3d01d7f290e895d2977028a984: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen21136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21137" type="x-p"/> That God was their rock - They recollected in their affliction that Jehovah was their Creator, and their Father; the Rock, the Source, not only of their being, but of all their blessings; or, that he was their sole Protector. <div eID="gen21137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21138" type="x-p"/> And the high God their Redeemer - ואל עליון גאלם veel elyon goalam, "And the strong God the Most High, their kinsman." That one who possessed the right of redemption; the nearest akin to him who had forfeited his inheritance; so the word originally means, and hence it is often used for a redeemer. The Hebrew word גאל goel answers to the Greek σωτηρ, a savior; and is given to the Lord Jesus Christ, the strong God, the Most High, the Redeemer of a lost world. After this verse there is the following Masoretic note: חצי הספר chatsi hassepher, "The middle of the book." And thus the reader has arrived at the middle of the Psalter, a book for excellence unparalleled.
entries.1f988e3c1459193a8b6d0ea28d47467f77f97d8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen21138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21139" type="x-p"/> Nevertheless they did flatter him with their mouth - What idea could such people have of God, whom they supposed they could thus deceive? They promised well, they called him their God, and their fathers' God; and told him how good, and kind, and merciful he had been to them. Thus, their mouth flattered him. And they said that, whatever the Lord their God commanded them to do, they would perform. <div eID="gen21139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21140" type="x-p"/> And they lied unto him - I think the Vulgate gives the true sense of the Hebrew: Dilexerunt eum in ore suo; et lingua sua mentiti Bunt ei, - "They loved him with their mouth; and they lied unto him with their tongue." "That is," says the old Psalter, "thai sayde thai lufed God, bot thai lighed, als thair dedes schewes; for thai do noght als thai hight; for when God ceses to make men rad; than cese thai to do wele."
entries.b77731625cfa6907a28071c2638c0e14ec4b51b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen21140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21141" type="x-p"/> Their heart was not right - When the heart is wrong, the life is wrong; and because their heart was not right with God, therefore they were not faithful in his covenant.
entries.a377c40728f11bdf1c0655e7289125375c9577c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen21141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21142" type="x-p"/> But he, being full of compassion - Feeling for them as a father for his children. <div eID="gen21142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21143" type="x-p"/> Forgave their iniquity - יחפר yechapper, made an atonement for their iniquity. <div eID="gen21143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21144" type="x-p"/> And did not stir up all his wrath - Though they often grieved his Spirit, and rebelled against him, yet he seldom punished them; and when he did chastise them, it was as a tender and merciful Father. He did not stir up all his wrath - the punishment was much less than the iniquity deserved.
entries.a3bb4311bbc6f13dbd89e64a74e74b017840e8c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen21144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21145" type="x-p"/> He remembered that they were but flesh - Weak mortals. He took their feeble perishing state always into consideration, and knew how much they needed the whole of their state of probation; and therefore he bore with them to the uttermost. How merciful is God! <div eID="gen21145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21146" type="x-p"/> A wind that passeth away, and cometh not again - I believe this to be a bad translation and may be productive of error; as if when a man dies his being were ended, and death were an eternal sleep. The original is, רוח הולך ולא ישוב ruach holech velo yashub: and the translation should be, "The spirit goeth away, and it doth not return." The present life is the state of probation; when therefore the flesh - the body, fails, the spirit goeth away into the eternal world, and returneth not hither again. Now God, being full of compassion, spared them, that their salvation might be accomplished before they went into that state where there is no change; where the pure are pure still, and the defiled are defiled still. All the Versions are right; but the polyglot translator of the Syriac, rocho, has falsely put ventus, wind, instead of spiritus, soul or spirit. The Arabic takes away all ambiguity: "He remembered that they were flesh; and a spirit which, when it departs, does not again return." The human being is composed of flesh and spirit, or body and soul; these are easily separated, and, when separated, the body turns to dust, and the spirit returns no more to animate it in a state of probation. Homer has a saying very like that of the psalmist: - Ανδρος δε ψυχη παλιν ελθειν ουτε ληἱστη, Ουθ' ἑλετη, επει αρ κεν αμειψεται ἑρκος οδοντων. <div eID="gen21146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21147" type="x-p"/> IL. ix., ver., 408. "But the soul of man returns no more; nor can it be acquired nor caught after it has passed over the barrier of the teeth." <div eID="gen21147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21148" type="x-p"/> Pope has scarcely given the passage its genuine meaning: - "But from our lips the vital spirit fled <div eID="gen21148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21149" type="x-p"/> Returns no more to wake the silent dead." <div eID="gen21149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21150" type="x-p"/> And the Ossian-like version of Macpherson is but little better: "But the life of man returns no more; nor acquired nor regained is the soul which once takes its flight on the wind." What has the wind to do with the ἑρκος οδοντων of the Greek poet? <div eID="gen21150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21151" type="x-p"/> Several similar sayings may be found among the Greek poets; but they all suppose the materiality of the soul.
entries.d993a4910d3633a709372e6cd3dad36d3539be59: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen21151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21152" type="x-p"/> Limited the Holy One of Israel - The Chaldee translates, "And the Holy One of Israel they signed with a sign." The Hebrew word התוו hithvu is supposed to come from the root תוה tavah, which signifies to mark; and hence the letter ת tau, which in the ancient Hebrew character had the form of a cross X, had its name probably because it was used as a mark. Mr. Bate observes that in hithpael it signifies to challenge or accuse; as one who gives his quark or pledge upon a trial, and causes his adversary to do the same. Here it most obviously means an insult offered to God.
entries.ef3445d53c4b38a8fa0f279e917c2c35f4a3dd46: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen21152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21153" type="x-p"/> Turned their rivers into blood - See on <reference osisRef="Exo.7.20">Exo 7:20</reference> (note).
entries.e3bdbc122753d9e4f58524d9517b822c5f47a82b: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen21153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21154" type="x-p"/> He sent - flies - and frogs - See on <reference osisRef="Exo.8.6">Exo 8:6</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Exo.8.24">Exo 8:24</reference> (note).
entries.9af417c08f12ccd6f6593962528dee949c160fa6: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen21154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21155" type="x-p"/> The caterpillar and - the locust - See on <reference osisRef="Exo.10.13">Exo 10:13</reference> (note).
entries.17d98c176a1a2f796a6a5d84fbdffb35ea06253e: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen21155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21156" type="x-p"/> He destroyed their vines with hail - Though the vine was never plentiful in Egypt, yet they have some; and the wine made in that country is among the most delicious. The leaf of the vine is often used by the Egyptians of the present day for wrapping up their mince-meat, which they lay leaf upon leaf, season it after their fashion, and so cook it, making it a most exquisite sort of food, according to Mr. Maillet. <div eID="gen21156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21157" type="x-p"/> And their sycamore-trees - This tree was very useful to the ancient Egyptians, as all their coffins are made of this wood; and to the modern, as their barques are made of it. Besides, it produces a kind of fig, on which the common people in general live; and Mr. Norden observes that "they think themselves well regaled when they have a piece of bread, a couple of sycamore figs, and a pitcher of water from the Nile." The loss therefore of their vines and sycamore-trees must have been very distressing to the Egyptians.
entries.604da9034c6cfea5e81bcfc5609e70f0ef2a4b05: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen21157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21158" type="x-p"/> He gave up their cattle - See on <reference osisRef="Exo.9.23">Exo 9:23</reference> (note).
entries.3bb4ba1c892d92752a17e88a3f51826bf5356beb: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen21158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21159" type="x-p"/> By sending evil angels - This is the first mention we have of evil angels. There is no mention of them in the account we have of the plagues of Egypt in the Book of Exodus, and what they were we cannot tell: but by what the psalmist says here of their operations, they were the sorest plague that God had sent; they were marks or the fierceness of his anger, wrath, indignation, and trouble. Some think the destroying angel that slew all the first-born is what is here intended; but this is distinctly mentioned in <reference osisRef="Psa.78.61">Psa 78:61</reference>. An angel or messenger may be either animate or inanimate; a disembodied spirit or human being; any thing or being that is an instrument sent of God for the punishment or support of mankind.
entries.72de99321cd255aa8122681c0153791080c4f332: <hi type="bold">Verse 54</hi> <div eID="gen21159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21160" type="x-p"/> The border of his sanctuary - קדשו kodsho, "of his holy place," that is, the land of Canaan, called afterwards the mountain which his right hand had purchased; because it was a mountainous country, widely differing from Egypt, which was a long, continued, and almost perfect level.
entries.d399ffb5e528f9e480e40f22c086beafedeef36a: <hi type="bold">Verse 57</hi> <div eID="gen21160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21161" type="x-p"/> They were turned aside like a deceitful bow - The eastern bow, which when at rest is in the form of a [curved figure], must be recurved, or turned the contrary way, in order to be what is called bent and strung. If a person who is unskilful or weak attempt to recurve and string one of these bows, if he take not great heed it will spring back and regain its quiescent position, and perhaps break his arm. And sometimes I have known it, when bent, to start aside, and regain its quiescent position, to my no small danger, and in one or two cases to my injury. This image is frequently used in the sacred writings; but no person has understood it, not being acquainted with the eastern bow [curved figure], which must be recurved, or bent the contrary way, [figure] in order to be proper for use. If not well made, they will fly back in discharging the arrow. It is said of the bow of Jonathan, it turned not back, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.22">2Sam 1:22</reference>, לא נשוג אחור lo nasog achor, "did not twist itself backward." It was a good bow, one on which he could depend. Hosea, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.16">Hos 7:16</reference>, compares the unfaithful Israelites to a deceitful bow; one that, when bent, would suddenly start aside and recover its former position. We may find the same passage in <reference osisRef="Jer.9.3">Jer 9:3</reference>. And this is precisely the kind of bow mentioned by Homer, Odyss. xxi., which none of Penelope's suitors could bend, called καμπυλα τοξα and αγκυλα τοξα, the crooked bow in the state of rest; but τοξον παλιντονον, the recurred bow when prepared for use. And of this trial of strength and skill in the bending of the bow of Ulysses, none of the critics and commentators have been able to make any thing, because they knew not the instrument in question. On the τοξου θησις of Homer, I have written a dissertation elsewhere. The image is very correct; these Israelites, when brought out of their natural bent, soon recoiled, and relapsed into their former state.
entries.4ff49560992fc3fc144c2bca26617b375542b3f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 60</hi> <div eID="gen21161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21162" type="x-p"/> He forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh - The Lord, offended with the people, and principally with the priests, who had profaned his holy worship, gave up his ark into the hands of the Philistines. And so true it is that he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, that he never returned to it again. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.1">1Sam 6:1</reference>; 2 Samuel 6; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.1">1Kgs 8:1</reference>; where the several removals of the ark are spoken of, and which explain the remaining part of this Psalm. Because God suffered the Philistines to take the ark, it is said, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.61">Psa 78:61</reference> : "He delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemy's hand;" and <reference osisRef="Psa.78.67">Psa 78:67</reference>, that "he refused the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim;" for Shiloh was in the tribe of Ephraim the son of Joseph; and God did not suffer his ark to return thither, but to go to Kirjath-jearim, which was in the tribe of Benjamin, from thence to the house of Obed-edom: and so to Zion in the tribe of Judah, as it follows, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.68">Psa 78:68</reference>. <div eID="gen21162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21163" type="x-p"/> The tabernacle which Moses had constructed in the wilderness remained at Shiloh even after the ark was taken by the Philistines and afterwards sent to Kirjath-jearim. From Shiloh it was transported to Nob; afterwards to Gibeon, apparently under the reign of Saul; and it was there at the commencement of Solomon's reign, for this prince went thither to offer sacrifices, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.4">1Kgs 3:4</reference>. From the time in which the temple was built, we know not what became of the tabernacle of Moses: it was probably laid up in some of the chambers of the temple. See Calmet.
entries.54a1af9741459adcc2cd03de8f16b2e34018292a: <hi type="bold">Verse 63</hi> <div eID="gen21163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21164" type="x-p"/> Their maidens were not given to marriage - הוללו hullalu, were not celebrated with marriage songs. It is considered a calamity in the east if a maiden arrives at the age of twelve years without being sought or given in marriage.
entries.de30e59c279dc5284d2f42c4d5a76a17fae1a004: <hi type="bold">Verse 64</hi> <div eID="gen21164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21165" type="x-p"/> Their priests fell by the sword - Hophni and Phinehas, who were slain in that unfortunate battle against the Philistines in which the ark of the Lord was taken, <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.11">1Sam 4:11</reference>. <div eID="gen21165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21166" type="x-p"/> A Chaldee Targum on this passage says, "In the time in which the ark of the Lord was taken by the Philistines, Hophni and Phinehas, the two priests, fell by the sword at Shiloh; and when the news was brought, their wives made no lamentation, for they both died the same day."
entries.8dda958bfbbb578b549883fa54be4ddc9f91f528: <hi type="bold">Verse 65</hi> <div eID="gen21166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21167" type="x-p"/> Then the Lord awaked - He seemed as if he had totally disregarded what was done to his people, and the reproach that seemed to fall on himself and his worship by the capture of the ark. <div eID="gen21167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21168" type="x-p"/> Like a mighty man - כגבור kegibbor, like a hero that shouteth by reason of wine. One who, going forth to meet his enemy, having taken a sufficiency of wine to refresh himself, and become a proper stimulus to his animal spirits shouts - gives the war-signal for the onset; impatient to meet the foe, and sure of victory. The idea is not taken from the case of a drunken man. A person in such a state would be very unfit to meet his enemy, and could have little prospect of conquest.
entries.ddf5b62a94fe32f9a05f76679aed47ea9f7f46ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 66</hi> <div eID="gen21168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21169" type="x-p"/> He smote his enemies in the hinder part - This refers to the hemorrhoids with which he afflicted the Philistines. See the note on <reference osisRef="1Sam.5.6-1Sam.5.10">1Sam 5:6-10</reference> (note).
entries.14f2ff09a7471329ec0208da1d487f94137d4250: <hi type="bold">Verse 67</hi> <div eID="gen21169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21170" type="x-p"/> He refused the tabernacle of Joseph - See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.78.60">Psa 78:60</reference> (note).
entries.bccf0151455dee984087c68c315ae2512c0b12c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 69</hi> <div eID="gen21170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21171" type="x-p"/> He built his sanctuary like high palaces - כמו רמים kemo ramim, which several of the Versions understand of the monoceros or rhinoceros. The temple of God at Jerusalem was the only one in the land, and stood as prominent on Mount Zion as the horn of the unicorn or rhinoceros does upon his snout. And there he established his ark, to go no more out as long as the temple should last. Before this time it was frequently in a migratory state, not only in the wilderness, but afterwards in the promised land. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.78.60">Psa 78:60</reference> (note).
entries.1e8013877ac26725bb849648eb7e488077425cfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 70</hi> <div eID="gen21171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21172" type="x-p"/> He chose David - See the account <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.11">1Sam 16:11</reference> (note), etc.
entries.c2a1408f314c1dd3a6a47736ea0a8252e7a3eddf: <hi type="bold">Verse 71</hi> <div eID="gen21172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21173" type="x-p"/> From following the ewes - Instances of this kind are not unfrequent in the ancient Greek and Roman history. Croesus said that Gypes, who was the first of his race, was a slave, and rose to sovereignty, succeeding his predecessor, of whose sheep he had been the pastor.
entries.722fe29035c6e9eeb55e51b62ae99443d8b25b0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 72</hi> <div eID="gen21173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21174" type="x-p"/> So he fed them - Here David is mentioned as having terminated his reign. He had fed the people, according to the integrity of his heart, for that was ever disposed to do the will of God in the administration of the kingdom: and his hand being skillful in war, he always led them out to victory against their enemies.  <chapter eID="Ps.78"/> <div eID="gen21174" type="x-p"/>

entries.103768db54f173540f28887244c94a1e8a73bb56: <div eID="gen9786" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Warning-Mirror of History from Moses to David</title> <div sID="gen9787" type="x-p"/> In the last verse of Ps 77 Israel appears as a flock which is led by Moses and Aaron; in the last verse of Psalms 78 as a flock which is led by David, of a pure heart, with judicious hands. Both Psalms also meet in thoughts and expressions, just as the לאסף of both leads one to expect. Psalms 78 is called <hi type="italic">Maskı̂l</hi>, <hi type="italic">a meditation</hi>. The word would also be appropriate here in the signification “a didactic poem.” For the history of Israel is recapitulated here from the leading forth out of Egypt through the time of the Judges down to David, and that with the practical application for the present age that they should cleave faithfully to Jahve, more faithfully than the rebellious generation of the fathers. After the manner of the Psalms of Asaph the Ephraimites are made specially prominent out of the whole body of the people, their disobedience as well as the rejection of Shiloh and the election of David, by which it was for ever at an end with the supremacy of Ephraim and also of his brother-tribe of Benjamin. <div eID="gen9787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9788" type="x-p"/> The old Asaphic origin of the Psalm has been contested: - (1) Because <reference osisRef="Ps.78.9">Psa 78:9</reference> may be referred to the apostasy of Ephraim and of the other tribes, that is to say, to the division of the kingdom. But this reference is capriciously imagined to be read in Psa 78:9. (2) Because the Psalm betrays a malice, indeed a national hatred against Ephraim, such as is only explicable after the apostasy of the ten tribes. But the alienation and jealousy between Ephraim and Judah is older than the rupture of the kingdom. The northern tribes, in consequence of their position, which was more exposed to contact with the heathen world, had already assumed a different character from that of Judah living in patriarchal seclusion. They could boast of a more excited, more martial history, one richer in exploit; in the time of the Judges especially, there is scarcely any mention of Judah. Hence Judah was little thought of by them, especially by powerful Ephraim, which regarded itself as the foremost tribe of all the tribes. From the beginning of Saul’s persecution of David, however, when the stricter principle of the south came first of all into decisive conflict for the mastery with the more lax principle of the Ephraimites, until the rebellion of Jeroboam against Solomon, there runs through the history of Israel a series of acts which reveal a deep reft between Judah and the other tribes, more especially Benjamin and Ephraim. Though, therefore, it were true that a tone hostile to Ephraim is expressed in the Psalm, this would not be any evidence against its old Asaphic origin, since the psalmist rests upon facts, and, without basing the preference of Judah upon merit, he everywhere contemplates the sin of Ephraim, without any Judaean boasting, in a connection with the sin of the whole nation, which involves all in the responsibility. Nor is <reference osisRef="Ps.78.69">Psa 78:69</reference> against Asaph the contemporary of David; for Asaph may certainly have seen the building of the Temple of Solomon as it towered upwards to the skies, and Caspari in his Essay on the Holy One of Israel (<hi type="italic">Luther. Zeitschrift</hi>, 1844, 3) has shown that even the divine name קדושׁ ישׂראל does not militate against him. We have seen in connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12">Psa 76:1-12</reference> how deeply imbued Isaiah’s language is with that of the Psalms of Asaph. It cannot surprise us of Asaph is Isaiah’s predecessor in the use of the name “the Holy One of Isreal.” The fact, however, that the writer of the Psalm takes the words and colours of his narration from all five books of the Pentateuch, with the exception of Leviticus, is not opposed to our view of the origin of the Pentateuch, but favourable to it. The author of the Book of Job, with whom in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.64">Psa 78:64</reference> he verbally coincides, is regarded by us as younger; and the points of contact with other Psalms inscribed “by David,” “by the sons of Korah,” and “by Asaph,” do not admit of being employed for ascertaining his time, since the poet is by no means an unindependent imitator. <div eID="gen9788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9789" type="x-p"/> The manner of representation which characterizes the Psalm becomes epical in its extension, but is at the same time concise after the sententious style. The separate historical statements have a gnome-like finish, and a gem-like elegance. The whole falls into two principal parts, vv. 1-37, vv. 38-72; the second part passes over from the God-tempting unthankfulness of the Israel of the desert to that of the Israel of Canaan. Every three strophes form one group. <div eID="gen9789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9790" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.1-Ps.78.11">Psa 78:1-11</reference> <div eID="gen9790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9791" type="x-p"/> The poet begins very similarly to the poet of Ps 49. He comes forward among the people as a preacher, and demands for his <hi type="italic">tôra</hi> a willing, attentive hearing. תּורה is the word for every human doctrine or instruction, especially for the prophetic discourse which sets forth and propagates the substance of the divine teaching. Asaph is a prophet, hence <reference osisRef="Ps.78.2">Psa 78:2</reference> is quoted in Mat 13:34. as ῥηθὲν διὰ τοῦ προφήτου.<note placement="foot">The reading διὰ Ἠσαΐ́ου τοῦ προφήτου is, although erroneous, nevertheless ancient; since even the Clementine Homilies introduce this passage as the language of Isaiah.</note> <div eID="gen9791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9792" type="x-p"/> He here recounts to the people their history מנּי־קדם, from that Egyptaeo-Sinaitic age of yore to which Israel’s national independence and specific position in relation to the rest of the world goes back. It is not, however, with the external aspect of the history that he has to do, but with its internal teachings. משׁל is an allegory or parable, παραβολή, more particularly the apophthegm as the characteristic species of poetry belonging to the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, and then in general a discourse of an elevated style, full of figures, thoughtful, pithy, and rounded. חידה is that which is entangled, knotted, involved, <hi type="italic">perlexe dictum</hi>. The poet, however, does not mean to say that he will literally discourse gnomic sentences and propound riddles, but that he will set forth the history of the fathers after the manner of a parable and riddle, so that it may become as a parable, i.e., a didactic history, and its events as marks of interrogation and nota-bene’s to the present age. The lxx renders thus: ἀνοίξω ἐν παραβολαῖς τὸ στόμα μου, φθέγξομαι προβλήματα ἀπ ̓ ἀρχῆς. Instead of this the Gospel by Matthew has: ἀνοίξω ἐν παραβολαῖς τὸ στόμα μου, ἐρεύξομαι κεκρυμμένα ἀπὸ καταβολῆς (κόσμου), and recognises in this language of the Psalm a prophecy of Christ; because it is moulded so appropriately for the mouth of Him who is the Fulfiller not only of the Law and of Prophecy, but also of the vocation of the prophet. It is the object-clause to נכחד, and not a relative clause belonging to the “riddles out of the age of yore,” that follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.3">Psa 78:3</reference> with אשׁר, for that which has been heard only becomes riddles by the appropriation and turn the poet gives to it. <reference osisRef="Ps.78.3">Psa 78:3</reference> begins a new period (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.27">Psa 69:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.1">Jer 14:1</reference>, and frequently): What we have heard, and in consequence thereof known, and what our fathers have told us (word for word, like <reference osisRef="Ps.44.1">Psa 44:1</reference>; Jdg 6:13), that will we not hide from their children (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.15.18">Job 15:18</reference>). The accentuation is perfectly correct. The <hi type="italic">Rebı̂a</hi> by מבניהם has a greater distinctive force than the <hi type="italic">Rebı̂a</hi> by אחרון (לדור); it is therefore to be rendered: telling to the later generation (which is just what is intended by the offspring of the fathers) the glorious deeds of Jahve, etc. The <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. ויּקם joins on to אשׁר עשׂה. Glorious deeds, proofs of power, miracles hath He wrought, and in connection therewith set up an admonition in Jacob, and laid down an order in Israel, which He commanded our fathers, viz., to propagate by tradition the remembrance of those mighty deeds (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.8">Exo 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.14">Exo 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.9">Deu 4:9</reference>, and other passages). להודיעם has the same object as והודעתּם in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.9">Deu 4:9</reference>; Jos 4:22. The matter in question is not the giving of the Law in general, as the purpose of which, the keeping of the laws, ought then to have been mentioned before anything else, but a precept, the purpose of which was the further proclamation of the <hi type="italic">magnalia Dei</hi>, and indirectly the promotion of trust in god and fidelity to the Law; cf. Psa 81:5., where the special precept concerning the celebration of the Feast of the Passover is described as a עדוּת laid down in Joseph. The following generation, the children, which shall be born in the course of the ages, were to know concerning His deeds, and also themselves to rise up (יקוּמוּ, not: come into being, like the יבאוּ of the older model-passage Ps 22:32) and to tell them further to their children, in order that these might place their confidence in god (שׂים כּסל, like שׁית מחסה in <reference osisRef="Ps.73.28">Psa 73:28</reference>), and might not forget the mighty deeds of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.17">Psa 118:17</reference>), and might keep His commandments, being warned by the disobedience of the fathers. The generation of the latter is called סורר וּמרה, just as the degenerate son that is to be stoned is called in Deu 21:18. הכין לבּו, to direct one’s heart, i.e., to give it the right direction or tendency, to put it into the right state, is to be understood after <reference osisRef="Ps.78.37">Psa 78:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.33">2Ch 20:33</reference>, Sir. 2:17. <div eID="gen9792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9793" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.9">Psa 78:9</reference>, which comes in now in the midst of this description, is awkward and unintelligible. The supposition that “the sons of Ephraim” is an appellation for the whole of Israel is refuted by Psa 78:67. The rejection of Ephraim and the election of Judah is the point into which the historical retrospect runs out; how then can “the sons of Ephraim” denote Israel as a whole? And yet what is here said of the Ephraimites also holds good of the Israelites in general, as <reference osisRef="Ps.78.57">Psa 78:57</reference> shows. The fact, however, that the Ephraimites are made specially conspicuous out of the “generation” of all Israel, is intelligible from the special interest which the Psalms of Asaph take in the tribes of Joseph, and here particularly from the purpose of practically preparing the way for the rejection of Shiloh and Ephraim related further on. In <reference osisRef="Ps.78.10">Psa 78:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.78.11">Psa 78:11</reference> the Ephraimites are also still spoken of; and it is not until <reference osisRef="Ps.78.12">Psa 78:12</reference>, with the words “in sight of their fathers,” that we come back again to the nation at large. The Ephraimites are called נושׁקי רומי־קשׁת in the sense of נושׁקי קשׁת רומי קשׁת; the two participial construct forms do not stand in subordination but in co-ordination, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jer 46:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.19">Deu 33:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.19">2Sa 20:19</reference>, just as in other instances also two substantives, of which one is the explanation of the other, are combined by means of the construct, <reference osisRef="Job.20.17">Job 20:17</reference>, cf. 2Ki 17:13 <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>. It is therefore: those who prepare the bow, i.e., those arming themselves therewith (נשׁק as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.2">1Ch 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.17">2Ch 17:17</reference>), those who cast the vow, i.e., those shooting arrows from the bow (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.29">Jer 4:29</reference>), cf. Böttcher, §728. What is predicated of them, viz., “they turned round” (הפך as in Jdg 20:39, Jdg 20:41), stands in contrast with this their ability to bear arms and to defend themselves, as a disappointed expectation. Is what is meant thereby, that the powerful warlike tribe of Ephraim grew weary in the work of the conquest of Canaan (Judg. 1), and did not render the services which might have been expected from it? Since the historical retrospect does not enter into details until <reference osisRef="Ps.78.12">Psa 78:12</reference> onwards, this especial historical reference would come too early here; the statement consequently must be understood more generally and, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.78.57">Psa 78:57</reference>, figuratively: Ephraim proved itself unstable and faint-hearted in defending and in conducting the cause of God, it gave it up, it abandoned it. They did not act as the covenant of God required of them, they refused to walk (ללכת, cf. ללכת, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.7">Ecc 1:7</reference>) within the limit and track of His Tôra, and forgot the deeds of God of which they had been eye-witnesses under Moses and under Joshua, their comrades of the same family.
entries.9e8ed6955a1629fe85a515fa29361e3c8488b374: <reference osisRef="Ps.78.12-Ps.78.25">Psa 78:12-25</reference> <div eID="gen9793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9794" type="x-p"/> It is now related how wonderfully God led the fathers of these Ephraimites, who behaved themselves so badly as the leading tribe of Israel, in the desert; how they again and again ever indulged sinful murmuring, and still He continued to give proofs of His power and of His loving-kindness. The (according to Num 13:22) very ancient <hi type="italic">Zoan</hi>(<hi type="italic">Tanis</hi>), ancient Egyptian <hi type="italic">Zane</hi>, Coptic <hi type="italic">G'ane</hi>, on the east bank of the Tanitic arm of the Nile, so called therefrom - according to the researches to which the Turin Papyrus No. 112 has led, identical with <hi type="italic">Avaris</hi> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Isa.19.11">Isa 19:11</reference>)<note placement="foot">The identity of Avaris and Tanis is in the meanwhile again become doubtful. <hi type="italic">Tanis</hi> was the Hyksos city, but <hi type="italic">Pelusium</hi> = <hi type="italic">Avaris</hi> the Hyksos fortress; vid., Petermann’s <hi type="italic">Mittheilungen</hi>, 1866, S. 296-298.</note>  - was the seat of the Hyksos dynasties that ruled in the eastern Delta, where after their overthrow Rameses II, the Pharaoh of the bondage, in order to propitiate the enraged mass of the Semitic population of Lower Egypt, embraced the worship of Baal instituted by King Apophis. The colossal sitting figure of Rameses II in the pillared court of the Royal Museum in Berlin, says Brugsch (<hi type="italic">Aus dem Orient</hi> ii. 45), is the figure which Rameses himself dedicated to the temple of Baal in Tanis and set up before its entrance. This mighty colossus is a contemporary of Moses, who certainly once looked upon this monument, when, as Ps 78 says, he “wrought wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan.” The psalmist, moreover, keeps very close to the Tôra in his reproduction of the history of the Exodus, and in fact so close that he must have had it before him in the entirety of its several parts, the Deuteronomic, Elohimistic, and Jehovistic. Concerning the rule by which it is appointed <hi type="italic">‛ā'sa phéle</hi>, vid., on Psa 52:5. The primary passage to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.78.13">Psa 78:13</reference></hi> (cf. נוזלים <reference osisRef="Ps.78.16">Psa 78:16</reference>) is Exo 15:8. נד is a pile, i.e., a piled up heap or mass, as in Psa 33:7. And <reference osisRef="Ps.78.14">Psa 78:14</reference> is the abbreviation of Exo 13:21. In Psa 78:15. the writer condenses into one the two instances of the giving of water from the rock, in the first year of the Exodus (Ex. 17) and in the fortieth year (Num. 20). The <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> יבקּע and the plural צרים correspond to this compression. רבּה is not an adjective (after the analogy of תּהום רבּה), but an adverb as in <reference osisRef="Ps.62.3">Psa 62:3</reference>; for the giving to drink needs a qualificative, but תהמות does not need any enhancement. ויּוצא has <hi type="italic">ı̂</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">ē</hi> as in Psa 105:43. <div eID="gen9794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9795" type="x-p"/> The fact that the subject is continued in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.17">Psa 78:17</reference> with ויּוסיפוּ without mention having been made of any sinning on the part of the generation of the desert, is explicable from the consideration that the remembrance of that murmuring is closely connected with the giving of water from the rock to which the names <hi type="italic">Massah u - Merı̂bah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Merı̂bath - Kadesh</hi> (cf. Num 20:13 with Num 27:14; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.51">Deu 32:51</reference>) point back: they went on (עוד) winning against Him, in spite of the miracles they experienced. למרות is syncopated from להמרות as in Isa 3:8. The poet in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.18">Psa 78:18</reference> condenses the account of the manifestations of discontent which preceded the giving of the quails and manna (Ex. 16), and the second giving of quails (Num. 11), as he has done the two cases of the giving of water from the rock in Psa 78:15. They tempted God by unbelievingly and defiantly demanding (לשׁאל, <hi type="italic">postulando</hi>, Ew. §280, <hi type="italic">d</hi>) instead of trustfully hoping and praying. בּלבבם points to the evil fountain of the heart, and לנפשׁם describes their longing as a sensual eagerness, a lusting after it. Instead of allowing the miracles hitherto wrought to work faith in them, they made the miracles themselves the starting-point of fresh doubts. The poet here clothes what we read in <reference osisRef="Exod.16.3">Exo 16:3</reference>; Num 11:4., <reference osisRef="Ps.21.5">Psa 21:5</reference>, in a poetic dress. In לעמּו the unbelief reaches it climax, it sounds like self-irony. On the co-ordinating construction “therefore Jahve heard it and was wroth,” cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Isa 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Isa 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Isa 50:2</reference>; Rom 6:17. The allusion is to the wrath-burning at Taberah (Tab'eera), Num 11:1-3, which preceded the giving of the quails in the second year of the Exodus. For it is obvious that <reference osisRef="Ps.78.21">Psa 78:21</reference> and Num 11:1 coincide, ויתעבר ואשׁ here being suggested by the ותבער־בם אשׁ eht yb d of that passage, and אף עלה being the opposite of ותשׁקע האשׁ in Psa 78:2. A conflagration broke out at that time in the camp, at the same time, however, with the breaking out of God’s anger. The nexus between the anger and the fire is here an outward one, whereas in Num 11:1 it is an internal one. The ground upon which the wrathful decree is based, which is only hinted at there, is here more minutely given in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.22">Psa 78:22</reference> : they believed not in Elohim (vid., Num 14:11), i.e., did not rest with believing confidence in Him, and trusted not in His salvation, viz., that which they had experienced in the redemption out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.13">Exo 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.2">Exo 15:2</reference>), and which was thereby guaranteed for time to come. Now, however, when Taberah is here followed first by the giving of the manna, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.23-Ps.78.25">Psa 78:23-25</reference>, then by the giving of the quails, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.26-Ps.78.29">Psa 78:26-29</reference>, the course of the events is deranged, since the giving of the manna had preceded that burning, and it was only the giving of the quails that followed it. This putting together of the two givings out of order was rendered necessary by the preceding condensation (in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.18-Ps.78.20">Psa 78:18-20</reference>) of the clamorous desire for a more abundant supply of food before each of these events. Notwithstanding Israel’s unbelief, He still remained faithful: He caused manna to rain down out of the opened gates of heaven (cf. “the windows of heaven,” <reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Gen 7:11</reference>; 2Ki 7:2; Mal 3:10), that is to say, in richest abundance. The manna is called corn (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.40">Psa 105:40</reference>, after <reference osisRef="Exod.16.4">Exo 16:4</reference>, it is called bread) of heaven, because it descended in the form of grains of corn, and supplied the place of bread-corn during the forty years. לחם אבּירים the lxx correctly renders ἄρτον ἀγγέλων (אבּירים = גּבּרי כח, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.20">Psa 103:20</reference>). The manna is called “bread of angels” (Wisd. 16:20) as being bread from heaven (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.24">Psa 78:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.40">Psa 105:40</reference>), the dwelling-place of angels, as being <hi type="italic">mann es - semâ</hi>, heaven’s gift, its Arabic name, - a name which also belongs to the vegetable manna which flows out of the <hi type="italic">Tamarix mannifera</hi> in consequence of the puncture of the <hi type="italic">Coccus manniparus</hi>, and is even at the present day invaluable to the inhabitants of the desert of Sinai. אישׁ is the antithesis to אבירים; for if it signified “every one,” אכלוּ would have been said (Hitzig). צידהּ as in <reference osisRef="Exod.12.39">Exo 12:39</reference>; לשׂבע as in <reference osisRef="Exod.16.3">Exo 16:3</reference>, cf. Psa 78:8.
entries.4fe506179cd6e6ded614a4f280d4c0a5f42e8d96: <reference osisRef="Ps.78.26-Ps.78.37">Psa 78:26-37</reference> <div eID="gen9795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9796" type="x-p"/> Passing over to the giving of the quails, the poet is thinking chiefly of the first occasion mentioned in Ex. 16, which directly preceded the giving of the manna. But the description follows the second: יסּע (He caused to depart, set out) after Num 11:31. “East” and “south” belong together: it was a south-east wind from the Aelanitic Gulf. “To rain down” is a figurative expression for a plentiful giving of dispensing from above. “Its camp, its tents,” are those of Israel, Num 11:31, cf. Exo 16:13. The תּעוה, occurring twice, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.29-Ps.78.30">Psa 78:29-30</reference> (of the object of strong desire, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.21.3">Psa 21:3</reference>), points to <hi type="italic">Kibroth - hattaavah</hi>, the scene of this carnal lusting; הביא is the transitive of the בּוא in Pro 13:12. In <reference osisRef="Ps.78.30-Ps.78.31">Psa 78:30-31</reference> even in the construction the poet closely follows Num 11:33 (cf. also זרוּ with לזרא, aversion, loathing, Num 11:20). The <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> unites what takes place simultaneously; a construction which presents the advantage of being able to give special prominence to the subject. The wrath of God consisted in the breaking out of a sickness which was the result of immoderate indulgence, and to which even the best-nourished and most youthfully vigorous fell a prey. When the poet goes on in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.32">Psa 78:32</reference> to say that in spite of these visitations (בּכל־זאת) they went on sinning, he has chiefly before his mind the outbreak of “fat” rebelliousness after the return of the spies, cf. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.78.32">Psa 78:32</reference></hi> with Num 14:11. And <reference osisRef="Ps.78.33">Psa 78:33</reference> refers to the judgment of death in the wilderness threatened at that time to all who had come out of Egypt from twenty years old and upward (Num 14:28-34). Their life devoted to death vanished from that time onwards בּהבל, in breath-like instability, and בּבּהלה, in undurable precipitancy; the mode of expression in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.11">Psa 31:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.1">Job 36:1</reference> suggests to the poet an expressive play of words. When now a special judgment suddenly and violently thinned the generation that otherwise was dying off, as in Num 21:6., then they inquired after Him, they again sought His favour, those who were still preserved in the midst of this dying again remembered the God who had proved Himself to be a “Rock” (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">Deu 32:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.18">Deu 32:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.37">Deu 32:37</reference>) and to be a “Redeemer” (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.16">Gen 48:16</reference>) to them. And what next? <reference osisRef="Ps.78.36-Ps.78.37">Psa 78:36-37</reference><note placement="foot">According to the reckoning of the Masora this <reference osisRef="Ps.78.36">Psa 78:36</reference> is the middle verse of the 2527 verses of the Psalter (Buxtorf, <hi type="italic">Tiberias</hi>, 1620, p. 133).</note> tell us what effect they gave to this disposition to return to God. They appeased Him with their mouth, is meant to say: they sought to win Him over to themselves by fair speeches, inasmuch as they thus anthropopathically conceived of God, and with their tongue they played the hypocrite to Him; their heart, however, was not sincere towards Him (עם like את in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.8">Psa 78:8</reference>), i.e., not directed straight towards Him, and they proved themselves not stedfast (πιστοί, or properly βέβαιοι) in their covenant-relationship to Him.
entries.9ead06fe7286fda64279dead81a570b5ba4b59ee: <reference osisRef="Ps.78.38-Ps.78.48">Psa 78:38-48</reference> <div eID="gen9796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9797" type="x-p"/> The second part of the Psalm now begins. God, notwithstanding, in His compassion restrains His anger; but Israel’s God-tempting conduct was continued, even after the journey through the desert, in Canaan, and the miracles of judgment amidst which the deliverance out of Egypt had been effected were forgotten. With והוּא in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference><note placement="foot">According to <hi type="italic">B. Kiddushin</hi> 30 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, this <reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference> is the middle one of the 5896 פסוקין, στίχοι, of the Psalter. According to <hi type="italic">B. Maccoth</hi> 22 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference>, and previously <reference osisRef="Deut.28.58-Deut.28.59">Deu 28:58-59</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.8">Deu 29:8</reference> [9], were recited when the forty strokes of the lash save one, which according to <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.24">2Co 11:24</reference> Paul received five times, were being counted out to the culprit.</note> begins an adversative clause, which is of universal import as far as ישׁהית, and then becomes historical. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference></hi> expands what lies in רחוּם: He expiates iniquity and, by letting mercy instead of right take its course, arrests the destruction of the sinner. With והרבּה (Ges. §§142, 2) this universal truth is supported out of the history of Israel. As this history shows, He has many a time called back His anger, i.e., checked it in its course, and not stirred up all His blowing anger (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.42.13">Isa 42:13</reference>), i.e., His anger in all its fulness and intensity. We see that <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference></hi> refers to His conduct towards Israel, then <reference osisRef="Ps.78.39">Psa 78:39</reference> follows with the ground of the determination, and that in the form of an inference drawn from such conduct towards Israel. He moderated His anger against Israel, and consequently took human frailty and perishableness into consideration. The fact that man is flesh (which not merely affirms his physical fragility, but also his moral weakness, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen 6:3</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Gen 8:21</reference>), and that, after a short life, he falls a prey to death, determines God to be long-suffering and kind; it was in fact sensuous desire and loathing by which Israel was beguiled time after time. The exclamation “how oft!” <reference osisRef="Ps.78.40">Psa 78:40</reference>, calls attention to the praiseworthiness of this undeserved forbearance. <div eID="gen9797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9798" type="x-p"/> But with <reference osisRef="Ps.78.41">Psa 78:41</reference> the record of sins begins anew. There is nothing by which any reference of this <reference osisRef="Ps.78.41">Psa 78:41</reference> to the last example of insubordination recorded in the Pentateuch, Num 35:1-9 (Hitzig), is indicated. The poet comes back one more to the provocations of God by the Israel of the wilderness in order to expose the impious ingratitude which revealed itself in this conduct. התוה is the causative of תּוה = Syriac <hi type="italic">tewā'</hi>, תּהא, to repent, to be grieved, lxx παρώξυναν. The miracles of the tie of redemption are now brought before the mind in detail, <hi type="italic">ad exaggerandum crimen tentationis Deu cum summa ingratitudine conjunctum</hi> (Venema). The time of redemption is called יום, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Gen 2:4</reference> the hexahemeron. שׂים אות (synon. עשׂה, נתן) is used as in Exo 10:2. We have already met with מנּי־צר in Psa 44:11. The first of the plagues of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.14-Exod.7.25">Exo 7:14-25</reference>), the turning of the waters into blood, forms the beginning in Psa 78:44. From this the poet takes a leap over to the fourth plague, the ערב (lxx κυνόμυια), a grievous and destructive species of fly (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.20-Exod.8.32">Exo 8:20-32</reference>), and combines with it the frogs, the second plague (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.1-Exod.8.15">Exo 8:1-15</reference>). צפרדּע is the lesser Egyptian frog, <hi type="italic">Rana Mosaica</hi>, which is even now called Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍfd‛ , ḍofda</hi>. Next in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.46">Psa 78:46</reference> he comes to the eighth plague, the locusts, חסיל (a more select name of the migratory locusts than ארבּה), <reference osisRef="Exod.10.1-Exod.10.20">Ex 10:1-20</reference>; the third plague, the gnats and midges, כּנּים, is left unmentioned in addition to the fourth, which is of a similar kind. For the chastisement by means of destructive living things is now closed, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.47">Psa 78:47</reference> follows the smiting with hail, the seventh plague, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.13">Ex 9:13</reference>-35. חנמל (with pausal , not <hi type="italic">ā</hi>, cf. in <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.2">Eze 8:2</reference> the similarly formed החשׁמלה) in the signification hoar-frost (πάχνη, lxx, Vulgate, Saadia, and Abulwalîd), or locusts (Targum כּזוּבא = חגב), or ants (J. D. Michaelis), does not harmonize with the history; also the hoar-frost is called כּפוּר, the ant נּמלה (collective in Arabic <hi type="italic">neml</hi>). Although only conjecturing from the context, we understand it, with Parchon and Kimchi, of hailstones or hail. With thick lumpy pieces of ice He smote down vines and sycamore-trees (<hi type="italic">Fayum</hi> was called in ancient Egyptian “the district of the sycamore”). הרג proceeds from the Biblical conception that the plant has a life of its own. The description of this plague is continued in Psa 78:48. Two MSS present לדּבר instead of לבּרד; but even supposing that רשׁפים might signify the fever-burnings of the pestilence (vid., on <reference osisRef="Hab.3.5">Hab 3:5</reference>), the mention of the pestilence follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.50">Psa 78:50</reference>, and the devastation which, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.9.19-Exod.9.22">Exo 9:19-22</reference>, the hail caused among the cattle of the Egyptians is in its right place here. Moreover it is expressly said in <reference osisRef="Exod.9.24">Exo 9:24</reference> that there was conglomerate fire among the hail; רשׁפים are therefore flaming, blazing lightnings.
entries.ae418912eab9764600eaab64be8f483ee48fa076: <reference osisRef="Ps.78.49-Ps.78.59">Psa 78:49-59</reference> <div eID="gen9798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9799" type="x-p"/> When these plagues rose to the highest pitch, Israel became free, and removed, being led by its God, into the Land of Promise; but it continued still to behave there just as it had done in the desert. The poet in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.49-Ps.78.51">Psa 78:49-51</reference> brings the fifth Egyptian plague, the pestilence (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.1-Exod.9.7">Exo 9:1-7</reference>), and the tenth and last, the smiting of the first-born (מכּת בּכרות), <reference osisRef="Exod.11.1">Exo 11:1</reference>, together. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.78.49">Psa 78:49</reference></hi> sounds like <reference osisRef="Job.20.23">Job 20:23</reference> (cf. below <reference osisRef="Ps.78.64">Psa 78:64</reference>). מלאכי רעים are not wicked angels, against which view Hengstenberg refers to the scriptural thesis of Jacobus Ode in his work <hi type="italic">De Angelis, Deum ad puniendos malos homines mittere bonos angelos et ad castigandos pios usurpare malos</hi>, but angels that bring misfortune. The mode of construction belongs to the chapter of the genitival subordination of the adjective to the substantive, like אשׁת רע, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.24">Pro 6:24</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7">1Sa 28:7</reference>; Num 5:18, Num 5:24; 1Ki 10:15; <reference osisRef="Jer.24.2">Jer 24:2</reference>, and the Arabic <hi type="italic">msjdu 'l - jâm‛</hi>, the mosque of the assembling one, i.e., the assembling (congregational) mosque, therefore: angels (not of the wicked ones = wicked angels, which it might signify elsewhere, but) of the evil ones = evil, misfortune-bringing angels (Ew. §287, <hi type="italic">a</hi>). The poet thus paraphrases the המּשׁחית that is collectively conceived in <reference osisRef="Exod.12.13">Exo 12:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.23">Exo 12:23</reference>; Heb 11:28. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.78.50">Psa 78:50</reference></hi> the anger is conceived of as a stream of fire, in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.78.50">Psa 78:50</reference></hi> death as an executioner, and in 50 <hi type="italic">c</hi> the pestilence as a foe. ראשׁית אונים (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.3">Gen 49:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.21.17">Deu 21:17</reference>) is that which had sprung for the first time from manly vigour (<hi type="italic">plur. intensivus</hi>). Egypt is called חם as in Ps 105 and <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10">Psa 111:1-10</reference> according to <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Gen 10:6</reference>, and is also called by themselves in ancient Egyptian <hi type="italic">Kemi</hi>, Coptic <hi type="italic">Chêmi, Kême</hi> (vid., Plutarch, <hi type="italic">De Iside et Osiride</hi>, ch. 33). When now these plagues which softened their Pharaoh went forth upon the Egyptians, God procured for His people a free departure, He guided flock-like (כּעדר like בּעדר, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.24">Jer 31:24</reference>, with <hi type="italic">Dag. implicitum</hi>), i.e., as a shepherd, the flock of His people (the favourite figure of the Psalms of Asaph) through the desert, - He led them safely, removing all terrors out of the way and drowning their enemies in the Red Sea, to His holy territory, to the mountain which (זה) His right hand had acquired, or according to the accents (cf. <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 104): to the mountain there (זה), which, etc. It is not Zion that is meant, but, as in the primary passage Exo 15:16., in accordance with the parallelism (although this is not imperative) and the usage of the language, which according to <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Isa 11:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.13">Isa 57:13</reference>, is incontrovertible, the whole of the Holy Land with its mountains and valleys (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.11.11">Deu 11:11</reference>). בּחבל נחלה is the poetical equivalent to בּנחלה, Num 34:2; Num 36:2, and frequently. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi> (here in the same syntactical position as in <reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Isa 48:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.41">Eze 20:41</reference>, and also <reference osisRef="Job.22.24">Job 22:24</reference> surely): He made them (the heathen, viz., as in <reference osisRef="Josh.23.4">Jos 23:4</reference> their territories) fall to them (viz., as the expression implies, by lot, בגורל) as a line of inheritance, i.e., (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.11">Psa 105:11</reference>) as a portion measured out as an inheritance. It is only in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.56">Psa 78:56</reference> (and not so early as <reference osisRef="Ps.78.41">Psa 78:41</reference>) that the narration passes over to the apostate conduct of the children of the generation of the desert, that is to say, of the Israel of Canaan. Instead of עדוריו from עדוּת, the word here is עדוריו from עדה (a derivative of עוּד, not יעד). Since the apostasy did not gain ground until after the death of Joshua and Eleazar, it is the Israel of the period of the Judges that we are to think of here. קשׁת רמיּה, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.57">Psa 78:57</reference>, is not: a bow of slackness, but: a bow of deceit; for the point of comparison, according to Hos 7:16, is its missing the mark: a bow that discharges its arrow in a wrong direction, that makes no sure shot. The verb רמה signifies not only to allow to hang down slack (cogn. רפה), but also, according to a similar conception to <hi type="italic">spe dejicere</hi>, to disappoint, deny. In the very act of turning towards God, or at least being inclined towards Him by His tokens of power and loving-kindness, they turned (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jer 2:21</reference>) like a vow that misses the mark and disappoints both aim and expectation. The expression in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.58">Psa 78:58</reference> is like <reference osisRef="Deut.32.16">Deu 32:16</reference>, Deu 32:21. שׁמע refers to their prayer to the Ba(a4lim (Jdg 2:11). The word התעבּר, which occurs three times in this Psalm, is a word belonging to Deuteronomy (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.26">Deu 3:26</reference>). <reference osisRef="Ps.78.59">Psa 78:59</reference> is purposely worded exactly like Psa 78:21. The divine purpose of love spurned by the children just as by the fathers, was obliged in this case, as in the former, to pass over into angry provocation.
entries.18c53e70ff92d12b92224024e3a0750b9f20fc60: <reference osisRef="Ps.78.60-Ps.78.72">Psa 78:60-72</reference> <div eID="gen9799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9800" type="x-p"/> The rejection of Shiloh and of the people worshipping there, but later on, when the God of Israel is again overwhelmed by compassion, the election of Judah, and of Mount Zion, and of David, the king after His own heart. In the time of the Judges the Tabernacle was set up in Shiloh (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.1">Jos 18:1</reference>); there, consequently, was the central sanctuary of the whole people, - in the time of Eli and Samuel, as follows from <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.1">1Sa 1:1</reference>, it had become a fixed temple building. When this building was destroyed is not known; according to Jdg 18:30., cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12-Jer.7.15">Jer 7:12-15</reference>, it was probably not until the Assyrian period. The rejection of Shiloh, however, preceded the destruction, and practically took place simultaneously with the removal of the central sanctuary to Zion; and was, moreover, even previously decided by the fact that the Ark of the covenant, when given up again by the Philistines, was not brought back to Shiloh, but set down in Kirjath Jearîm (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2">1Sa 7:2</reference>). The attributive clause שׁכּן בּאדם uses שׁכּן as השׁכּין is used in Jos 18:1. The pointing is correct, for the words to not suffice to signify “where He dwelleth among men” (Hitzig); consequently שׁכּן is the causative of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.16">Lev 16:16</reference>; Jos 22:19. In <reference osisRef="Ps.78.61">Psa 78:61</reference> the Ark of the covenant is called the might and glory of God (ארון עזּו, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.8">Psa 132:8</reference>, cf. כבוד, 1Sa 4:21.), as being the place of their presence in Israel and the medium of their revelation. Nevertheless, in the battle with the Philistines between Eben-ezer and Aphek, Jahve gave the Ark, which they had fetched out of Shiloh, into the hands of the foe in order to visit on the high-priesthood of the sons of Ithamar the desecration of His ordinances, and there fell in that battle 30,000 footmen, and among them the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, the priests (1 Sam. 4). The fire in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.63">Psa 78:63</reference> is the fire of war, as in Num 21:28, and frequently. The incident mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.19">1Sa 6:19</reference> is reasonably (vid., Keil) left out of consideration. By לא הוּלּלוּ (lxx erroneously, οὐκ ἐπένθησαν = הוללוּ = הילילוּ) are meant the marriage-songs (cf. Talmudic הלּוּלא, the nuptial tent, and בּית הלוּלים the marriage-house). “Its widows (of the people, in fact, of the slain) weep not” (word for word as in <reference osisRef="Job.27.15">Job 27:15</reference>) is meant of the celebration of the customary ceremony of mourning (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.2">Gen 23:2</reference>): they survive their husbands (which, with the exception of such a case as that recorded in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.19-1Sam.14.22">1Sa 14:19-22</reference>, is presupposed), but without being able to show them the last signs of honour, because the terrors of the war (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.8">Jer 15:8</reference>) prevent them. <div eID="gen9800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9801" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Ps.78.65">Psa 78:65</reference> the song takes a new turn. After the punitive judgment has sifted and purified Israel, God receives His people to Himself afresh, but in such a manner that He transfers the precedence of Ephraim to the tribe of Judah. He awakes as it were from a long sleep (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.24">Psa 44:24</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.73.20">Psa 73:20</reference>); for He seemed to sleep whilst Israel had become a servant to the heathen; He aroused Himself, like a hero exulting by reason of wine, i.e., like a hero whose courage is heightened by the strengthening and exhilarating influence of wine (Hengstenberg). התרונן is not the <hi type="italic">Hithpal</hi>. of רוּן in the Arabic signification, which is alien to the Hebrew, to conquer, a meaning which we do not need here, and which is also not adapted to the reflexive form (Hitzig, without any precedent, renders thus: who allows himself to be conquered by wine), but <hi type="italic">Hithpo</hi>. of רנן: to shout most heartily, after the analogy of the reflexives התאונן, התנודד, התרועע. The most recent defeat of the enemy which the poet has before his mind is that of the Philistines. The form of expression in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.66">Psa 78:66</reference> is moulded after 1Sa 5:6. God smote the Philistines most literally <hi type="italic">in posteriora</hi> (lxx, Vulgate, and Luther). Nevertheless <reference osisRef="Ps.78.66">Psa 78:66</reference> embraces all the victories under Samuel, Saul, and David, from <reference osisRef="1Sam.5.1-1Sam.5.12">1Sa 5:1-12</reference> and onwards. Now, when they were able to bring the Ark, which had been brought down to the battle against the Philistines, to a settled resting-place again, God no longer chose Shiloh of Ephraim, but Judah and the mountain of Zion, which He had loved (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">Psa 47:5</reference>), of Benjamitish-Judaean (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.63">Jos 15:63</reference>; Jdg 1:8, Jdg 1:21) - but according to the promise (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">Deu 33:12</reference>) and according to the distribution of the country (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28">Psa 68:28</reference>) Benjamitish - Jerusalem.<note placement="foot">According to <hi type="italic">B. Menachoth</hi> 53 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, Jedidiah (Solomon, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.25">2Sa 12:25</reference>) built the Temple in the province of Jedidiah (of Benjamin, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">Deu 33:12</reference>).</note> <div eID="gen9801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9802" type="x-p"/> There God built His Temple כּמו־רמים. Hitzig proposes instead of this to read כּמרומים; but if נעימים, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">Psa 16:6</reference>, signifies <hi type="italic">amaena</hi>, then רמים may signify <hi type="italic">excelsa</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.45.2">Isa 45:2</reference> הדוּרים, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.6">Jer 17:6</reference> חררים) and be poetically equivalent to מרומים: lasting as the heights of heaven, firm as the earth, which He hath founded for ever. Since the eternal duration of heaven and of the earth is quite consistent with a radical change in the manner of its duration, and that not less in the sense of the Old Testament than of the New (vid., e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa 65:17</reference>), so the לעולם applies not to the stone building, but rather to the place where Jahve reveals Himself, and to the promise that He will have such a dwelling-place in Israel, and in fact in Judah. Regarded spiritually, i.e., essentially, apart from the accidental mode of appearing, the Temple upon Zion is as eternal as the kingship upon Zion with which the Psalm closes. The election of David gives its impress to the history of salvation even on into eternity. It is genuinely Asaphic that it is so designedly portrayed how the shepherd of the flock of Jesse (Isai) became the shepherd of the flock of Jahve, who was not to pasture old and young in Israel with the same care and tenderness as the ewe-lambs after which he went (עלות as in <reference osisRef="Gen.33.13">Gen 33:13</reference>, and רעה ב, cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.11">1Sa 16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34">1Sa 17:34</reference>, like משׁל בּ and the like). The poet is also able already to glory that he has fulfilled this vocation with a pure heart and with an intelligent mastery. And with this he closes. <div eID="gen9802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9803" type="x-p"/> From the decease of David lyric and prophecy are retrospectively and prospectively turned towards David.  <chapter eID="Ps.78"/> <div eID="gen9803" type="x-p"/>
